newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia seeks fix on back wages as protest looms.
newsitem.headline: Russia seeks fix on back wages as protest looms.

text.p: Russian officials on Tuesday said they were working round the clock to complete a cabinet reshuffle and deal with trade union demands before protests on Thursday which unions expect to draw 20 million people.
Government spokesman Igor Shabdurasulov said officials were working intensively to address trade union demands for payment of wage and pension arrears and finalise government changes.
"In the last two weeks, large parts of the government have worked round-the-clock in connection with the reorganisation of the government and the union protests on March 27," he said.

Trade union leaders said they expected more than 20 million people to turn out nationwide, including seven million strikers, to participate in Thursday's planned pickets, rallies and marches to protest against chronic wage arrears.
Workers are owed over 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion) in back wages, of which the state owes 10 trillion.

The government said it would unveil its latest plans on Wednesday afternoon at a news conference by a troika of top officials, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, and First Deputy Prime Ministers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov.
Chubais and Nemtsov, the two top appointees to the new government, have both pledged to speed up economic reform.
Before their Wednesday press conference, the two reformers and Chernomyrdin are scheduled to meet President Boris Yeltsin on the back wages problem.
"I consider the situation with the mass delays in wage payments unbearable," Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky quoted the president as saying.
Russia cannot immediately pay off its debts, but it can detail its approach to the problem.

"I wouldn't expect any revolutionary decisions in the next three to five days, two weeks, or even month on issues such as natural monopolies, social issues or other problems," Shabdurasulov told reporters. "It's not real to imagine solving such a series of problems tomorrow or the day after tomorrow."
He said it was absurd to hope that all back wages could be paid before Thursday, but said a timetable was being organised to set out realistic goals.
Back pensions would be paid by the end of June, debts to teachers by May, and government debts by the autumn.
It remained unclear to what extent Thursday's day-long protest would succeed, but Shabdurasulov said a small number of groups were ready to mar the event with violence.
Organisers said they had taken special security measures to maintain order. Previous efforts at organised protest have often failed to rally much support.

Grigory Yavlinsky, head of the liberal Yabloko party, told journalists he hoped Russians would support the protest actions to show their disapproval of government policy. He also said Yabloko would not join the new government team.
While grappling with domestic problems, Russia's political leaders have also been busy on the diplomatic front with meetings with senior officials from China and India.
Yeltsin met Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Tuesday and said Moscow was committed to close relations with New Delhi.
"We have been friends for many decades and we remain friends," Yeltsin said. "India remains a stabilising force in its region."
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, who came to prepare a visit by Chinese President Ziang Zemin planned for late April, also met Yeltsin.

Deve Gowda and Qian are visiting Moscow days after Yeltsin and Clinton "agreed to disagree" at their meeting in Helsinki over NATO's plans to invite former Soviet bloc states in eastern Europe to join the Western defence alliance.
